message.content:
Triangulation metrics are quantitative measures that describe the quality, performance, or characteristics of a triangulation run—typically a computational geometry operation that subdivides a region into triangles. In practice, these metrics help you assess how well the triangulation meets your goals (e.g., accuracy, efficiency, or mesh quality). Common categories include: | Category | Typical Metrics | What they tell you | |----------|-----------------|--------------------| | **Geometric Quality** | • Minimum/maximum angle
• Aspect ratio
• Edge length distribution
• Triangle area distribution | Indicates how “well‑shaped” the triangles are; helps avoid skinny or degenerate elements that can degrade numerical stability. | | **Coverage / Completeness** | • Total area covered
• Number of triangles
• Vertex count | Shows whether the triangulation fully covers the intended domain and how dense it is. | | **Error / Accuracy** | • Hausdorff distance to reference shape
• Mean squared error (MSE)
• Interpolation error | Measures how closely the triangulated surface approximates the underlying data or model. | | **Performance / Resource Usage** | • Runtime (seconds/minutes)
• Memory consumption (MB)
• CPU/GPU utilization | Helps evaluate the computational cost of generating the triangulation. | | **Topological Properties** | • Connectivity (number of connected components)
• Presence of holes or dangling edges | Ensures the mesh topology is valid for downstream processing (e.g., finite element analysis). | In many software systems, a “triangulation metrics” function will gather one or more of these statistics from a completed triangulation run and return them in a structured format (JSON, CSV, etc.). This allows users to compare different runs, tune algorithms, or validate that the output meets required standards.
